title: What C# is (compared to JavaScript and TypeScript)
hook: C# is a compiled language whose types stay real at run time. JavaScript runs in engines like V8, and TypeScript only checks types before they disappear. Knowing which host runs your code prevents costly mix-ups in interviews and on the job.

blocks.text: C# is a statically typed language built for the .NET platform. When you write C#, a compiler turns your source into Intermediate Language (IL) packaged with metadata. The Common Language Runtime (CLR) loads that output and runs it. JavaScript is what browsers and Node.js execute directly (often after just-in-time compilation inside an engine like V8). TypeScript adds type checking on top of JavaScript, but those types are erased before anything runs — the engine never sees them.

entries.plainDefinition: The shared type rules every .NET language follows so types from C#, F#, and others can work together.
entries.example: An int in C# maps to the same CTS type that other .NET languages understand.

entries.plainDefinition: The .NET run-time host that loads assemblies, enforces types, manages memory, and executes your code.
entries.example: A .NET worker or Lambda runs on the CLR, not on Node.js.

entries.plainDefinition: A CPU-neutral instruction set that .NET compilers emit before the runtime turns it into machine code.
entries.example: Your .cs file becomes IL inside a .dll file.

blocks.text: If you treat C# like "TypeScript that compiles to something else," you will misunderstand errors, performance, and deployment. A Redis client in C# holds a real typed object at run time. A TypeScript interface describes shape only until JavaScript runs. When you ship an Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) consumer as a .NET Lambda, the host is the CLR — not Node.js. Same JSON event, different process, different type system, different garbage collector.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: C# compiles to IL for the CLR with real types. TypeScript type-checks then erases. JavaScript is what the engine executes. Three different layers — do not collapse them.

items.title: You write C#
items.body: The compiler checks every variable against a real type (int, string, your own classes).

items.title: Roslyn emits IL + metadata
items.body: Types are written into the assembly. They survive after compile — unlike TypeScript types.

items.title: CLR loads and runs
items.body: The runtime verifies the assembly, Just-In-Time (JIT) compiles methods to CPU code, and enforces type safety.

diagram.title: C# vs JavaScript/TypeScript hosts
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph csharp [C# path]
    CS[C# source] --> Roslyn[Roslyn compiler]
    Roslyn --> IL[IL + metadata]
    IL --> CLR[CLR host]
    CLR --> CPU[Machine code]
  end
  subgraph jsts [JS/TS path]
    TS[TypeScript optional] --> JS[JavaScript source]
    JS --> V8[V8 or other engine]
    V8 --> CPU2[Machine code]
  end

sections.heading: Code walkthrough: types that survive compile

snippet.label: Types stay after compile
snippet.explanation: The compiler rejects assigning a bool to attemptCount. After publish, the CLR still sees Int32. A TypeScript number would have been erased to an IEEE-754 JavaScript number.

snippet.label: Run-time type information exists
snippet.explanation: C# values carry run-time type data the CLR can inspect. This powers reflection, serialization, and safe casting — things TypeScript types alone cannot provide.

snippet.label: TypeScript erases at compile time
snippet.explanation: TypeScript interfaces exist only for the checker. C# interfaces and classes are real types in the assembly the CLR loads.

blocks.title: C# vs JavaScript/TypeScript at a glance
rows: TypeScript: compile time only; JS: dynamic

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Saying C# is "just Java with a different runtime" and skipping the Common Type System (CTS) and CLR. Assuming tsc is analogous to dotnet build — tsc erases types; the C# compiler emits typed IL. Calling a .NET Lambda handler "Node-like" because both receive JSON — the deserializer still produces CLR objects with real types.

interviewTakeaways: Name three layers: C# language, CTS/BCL types, CLR host.
TypeScript does not give you a CLR; Node Lambdas are a different host from .NET Lambdas.
C# is in the C family for braces and semicolons, but value types, privacy, and IL metadata are not JavaScript semantics.
commonPitfalls: Saying C# is "just Java with a different runtime" and skipping CTS/CLR.
Assuming `tsc` is analogous to `dotnet build` — tsc erases; the C# compiler emits typed IL.
Calling the Lambda handler "Node-like" because both use JSON events. The deserializer and types are still CLR objects.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript types exist only at compile time. C# types remain as metadata the CLR uses for safety, reflection, and interop.
Node executes JavaScript on V8. A .NET worker or Lambda executes IL on the CLR. Same SQS payload, different process and type system.
